1219.title: The world as dream
1219.hook: a dream, a show, a bubble on water: the ninth Guru's pictures of a passing world
1219.howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks, with their images of the world as a dream and a bubble, are read near the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, including the readings families hold after a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the traveler's hymns: O mind, take shelter. Your line was prayer on the road.

There's a half second, just after a vivid dream, when the dream is still the real world. The argument is still going. The house is still that strange house. Then the ceiling comes into focus, a car passes outside, and the whole thing drains away like water from a sink. Nothing in it was lost, because none of it was ever held. Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Tegh Bahadur keeps coming back to that half second. Again and again, his saloks hold up the world and say: look, a dream.
screen: `THE HALF SECOND AFTER A DREAM.` → `IT DRAINS AWAY.` → `THE GURU: LOOK, A DREAM.`

segments.voice: Two of his saloks, paraphrased. The first: know this world as a dream and a passing show; in it, Nanak, nothing is true except the Lord. The second: as a bubble rises on water and bursts, again and again, so the world is made; listen, friend, says Nanak. A dream, a show, a bubble: real enough to see, too quick to keep. Here's what the dream does not mean. It doesn't mean nothing matters. The same Guru stayed a householder, traveled to visit his Sikhs, and stood up for other people's faith with his life. You don't do that for a world you think is worthless. One way Sikhs read these saloks: the dream is real as a dream. People, work, love, all of it is worth doing. What's untrue is the idea that any of it will stay. The mistake isn't living in the dream; it's clutching at it, as if the bubble could go in a pocket. And the cure isn't to tear the world down. It's to wake up: to notice, while you're still inside it, that the One who is true was there all along. A slammed alarm clock wakes you angry. A curtain opened slowly wakes you well. The saloks open the curtain one line at a time. And if life ever feels like it doesn't matter at all, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `A DREAM, A SHOW, A BUBBLE.` · `IT DOESN'T MEAN NOTHING MATTERS.` · `THE MISTAKE IS CLUTCHING.` · `A CURTAIN, NOT AN ALARM.` · then, large: `WAKE UP GENTLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been gripping hard, a plan, a worry, a grudge, a thing you want badly, and don't throw it away. Look at it the way you'd look at a dream you're slowly waking from, real while it lasts, not forever, and with each breath out let the room come into focus around it. If you pray, rest in Waheguru, the one the saloks call true.
The world as dream. In the ninth Guru's saloks, the world is a dream, a show, a bubble on water, and nothing in it stays except the Lord. Today's word.
Your line: wake up gently. A curtain opened slowly, never a slammed alarm. Rest well.

1220.title: The Name that remains
1220.hook: kings and their enemies pass; the ninth Guru names what stays
1220.howItsDone: These saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur are read near the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs practice naam simran, remembering the Name, by repeating Waheguru and singing gurbani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the world as dream: a show, a bubble on water. Your line was wake up gently.

Everyone in this photograph is gone now. It came out of a box in a closet: a wedding, maybe, or a family on a porch. The porch is gone. The clothes, the car, the town as it looked. On the back, in faded pencil, somebody wrote down who they were. Of everything in that picture, the writing has outlasted the people. Yesterday the ninth Guru called the world a dream. Today, near the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib, he names what doesn't drain away when you wake.
screen: `AN OLD PHOTOGRAPH IN A BOX.` → `EVERYONE IN IT IS GONE.` → `WHAT DOESN'T DRAIN AWAY?`

segments.voice: Two saloks, side by side, paraphrased. The first: Ram has gone, and Ravan has gone, though he had a great family; nothing is fixed, says Nanak, the world is like a dream. Ram and Ravan, the hero and the enemy of the Ramayana, a story Hindus hold sacred. Even the kings of that story, on both sides, passed from the earth. Then the turn. The second salok: the Name has remained; the holy ones have remained; the Guru, the Lord of the world, has remained. And a question: says Nanak, who in this world has truly repeated the Guru's mantra? So here's what stays. Not palaces, families or kingdoms. The Name, which Sikhs understand as the presence of God, remembered and repeated. The holy ones, the company of people who live that remembering. And the Guru, the Lord, the source of it all. The pencil on the photograph lasts a while, then fades too. The Name in this salok isn't writing on paper. It's what a life is pointed toward. When Sikhs remember the Name, saying Waheguru, singing the hymns, keeping it under the breath through a working day, they're touching the one thing the Guru says isn't part of the dream. That closing question is honest, not proud. The Guru doesn't claim everyone remembers; he asks who has. Some readers hear a quiet invitation in it: be one who does, once more today. If a loss is heavy on you right now, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `RAM AND RAVAN HAVE GONE.` · `THE NAME, THE HOLY, THE GURU REMAIN.` · `NOT WRITING ON PAPER.` · `WHO HAS REPEATED THE MANTRA?` · then, large: `IT REMAINS.`

segments.voice: Let the passing things of your day drift by, the inbox, the dishes, the news, like pictures in a closet box. Then come back to one thing that stays: if you pray, repeat Waheguru quietly once on each breath; if not, choose one word for what lasts for you and return to it whenever the mind wanders. Once more, and once more.
The Name that remains. When kings, families and kingdoms pass, the ninth Guru's salok says the Name, the holy ones and the Guru remain. Today's word.
Your line: it remains. Whatever passes, the Name still stays. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1221.title: The Gurus' teachings close
1221.hook: five Gurus, one signature: looking back at Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, Arjan and Tegh Bahadur
1221.howItsDone: In the Guru Granth Sahib each Guru's hymns carry a Mahala heading with a number, and are signed Nanak; Sikhs read and sing them together as one Guru's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Name that remains, when Ram and Ravan have gone. Your line was it remains.

Here's a small thing on the page that's easy to miss. When the Gurus sign their hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib, they use one name: Nanak. Guru Angad signs as Nanak. So do Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjan, and the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur. How do readers tell them apart? Above each hymn sits a heading: Mahala, with a number. One, two, three, four, five, nine. Different hands, different generations, one name. Today closes this stretch of the path by listening to them all at once.
screen: `ONE SIGNATURE: NANAK.` → `MAHALA ONE, TWO, THREE, FOUR, FIVE, NINE.` → `LISTEN TO THEM ALL AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Start with Guru Angad, the quiet successor. Few words, deep. He called the Guru a light where all was dark, warned against service mixed with pride, and called ego an illness with the cure inside it. Then Guru Amar Das: O mind, you are the form of light. The world is burning; save it by any door. Not the pyre, but a faithful life. And a kitchen open to all. Then Guru Ram Das: the Gursikh's morning, rising early, remembering, then going to work still remembering. Wedding songs of the soul riding to the Beloved. A city where the market itself could be holy. Then Guru Arjan: an alphabet that ends in grace, a plate of truth, contentment and reflection, what You do seems sweet to me, serving the One, and a book chosen carefully, with room for saints from outside the line of Gurus. And last, the ninth Guru: neither fear nor frighten, home held lightly, their faith, their right, level, a dream, a bubble, and the Name that remains. Hear how different they sound: a spare one-liner, a burning world, a wedding song, a long alphabet, a calm verse tradition hears through his last days. And yet it's one teaching: the One, the Name, the turning from ego toward the Guru. Sikhs hear that oneness in the shared signature, Nanak, and speak of one light passing from Guru to Guru, the way a lamp lights a lamp. The flame looks different in each lamp. It's the same flame.
screen: `ANGAD: SHORT AND SHARP.` · `AMAR DAS AND RAM DAS: LIGHT, KITCHEN, CITY.` · `ARJAN AND THE NINTH: SWEET, LEVEL, REMAINING.` · `ONE LIGHT, LAMP TO LAMP.` · then, large: `ONE TEACHING, MANY VOICES.`

segments.voice: Let the five Gurus pass by one at a time, like singers taking turns: Guru Angad, short and sharp; Guru Amar Das, the open kitchen; Guru Ram Das, the morning; Guru Arjan, sweetness; Guru Tegh Bahadur, the level heart. Notice which voice you lean toward, with no wrong answer, and hold one line of theirs to come back to. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath.
The Gurus' teachings close. From the second Guru to the fifth, and the ninth: different voices, one signature, one teaching. Today's word.

1222.title: The Tenth Guru's book
1222.hook: compiled after his death, traditionally by Bhai Mani Singh; its make-up is discussed respectfully among Sikhs
1222.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Jaap Sahib and verses from Akal Ustat, both found in the Dasam Granth, among their daily prayers; the Guru Granth Sahib alone is installed and honored as the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Gurus' teachings closed, from the second Guru through the fifth, and the ninth. Your line was one teaching, many voices.

Some books are finished by their authors. Others are finished by the people who loved them. A teacher dies, and a student goes from house to house, collecting copies of what was written, sorting them, setting them in order. The book that comes out of it is treasured. Because the teacher didn't set the order himself, readers can ask, gently, which page came from which hand. A new block of the path starts today, the writings of Guru Gobind Singh, and it starts with a book like that.
screen: `FINISHED BY THOSE WHO LOVED HIM.` → `COPIES GATHERED, SET IN ORDER.` → `WHICH PAGE, WHICH HAND?`

segments.voice: Its name is Dasam Granth: the book of the Tenth. You first heard that name on day eighty-three, at a court of poets in Anandpur. It holds writings associated with Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition says it was compiled after his death, and it names Bhai Mani Singh, a learned Sikh of the Guru's circle, as the one who gathered it. So it was not set in order by the Guru himself the way the Adi Granth was set in order by Guru Arjan. That difference matters, and Sikhs keep it in view. Inside, some of it Sikhs pray every day: Jaap Sahib, and verses from Akal Ustat, are among the morning prayers of the Sikh daily round, and tradition places some of its prayers at the Khalsa initiation. There is Bachitar Natak, a poem that tells parts of his own story. There is the Zafarnama, a letter in Persian. And there are long retellings of old Indian tales that read very differently from the hymns. The Guru Granth Sahib is the Guru for Sikhs; the Dasam Granth is not. Sikhs discuss which parts of the Dasam Granth come from the Guru's own pen. Some hold that all of it does. Some hold that the prayers clearly do and other parts may come from poets in his court. At its best, that discussion keeps a careful tone, because it's about a beloved teacher's words. Nobody on this path will be told which side to take. For the next weeks, this path reads the parts Sikhs pray and quote, and says plainly when a question is open.

1223.title: Akal Ustat
1223.hook: praise of the Timeless One in many meters
1223.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Tav Prasad swayyas from Akal Ustat as part of their morning prayers, and stanzas of Akal Ustat are sung as kirtan in gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dasam Granth, the book of the Tenth, and the care Sikhs bring to talking about its make-up. Your line was discussed with respect.

A marching drum. Then a lullaby. Then a fast, tumbling chant, the kind that makes your tongue work. Then something slow enough to walk to. If a single poem changed its rhythm that often, you'd expect it to change its subject too. This one doesn't. Every beat, every speed, points at the same One. It sits inside the Dasam Granth, and Sikhs pray parts of it in the morning. Its name is a description of what it does.
screen: `A DRUM, A LULLABY, A CHANT.` → `ONE SUBJECT THROUGH IT ALL.` → `A NAME THAT SAYS WHAT IT DOES.`

segments.voice: Akal Ustat: praise of the Timeless One. Akal is the One beyond time, the One that death and change don't reach. Ustat is praise. The poem moves through many meters, many verse forms, as if every rhythm in the poet's ear had to take a turn. It opens with a line of shelter, given here in paraphrase: the Timeless Being is my protector; the All-Steel is my protector. All-Steel, Sarab Loh, is a name for God that sounds like a blade, the strength that doesn't bend. So praise begins by leaning. Before anything grand, it says: I'm held. Then come the stanzas recited in the Sikh morning prayers, the swayyas called Tav Prasad. A long parade, in paraphrase: I have seen the pure and the holy men, ascetics and yogis. I have seen mighty kings with elephants and banners, armies stretching away. I have seen pilgrims bathing at sacred places. And then the turn that comes back again and again: without the love of the Lord, without His grace, all of it counts for nothing. One stanza ends with a line tradition holds dear, again in paraphrase: I speak the truth, all of you, listen; only those who loved have found the Lord. That's the engine of the poem. It doesn't mock kings or pilgrims. It walks past them with open eyes and says that the Timeless One is reached by love, not by size. Praise, in Akal Ustat, isn't flattery. It's a way of putting things back in their right scale: the armies are small, and the One is not.

1224.title: One human race
1224.hook: recognize all humankind as one (Akal Ustat 85)
1224.howItsDone: Sikhs quote 'manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo' from Akal Ustat when speaking about equality, and it is lived out in langar, where everyone eats together seated in the same rows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akal Ustat, the poem that walks past kings and pilgrims and says the Lord is found by love. Your line was praise of the timeless.

Forms ask. Box one, box two, box three. Religion, caste, nationality, community. Hospital intake sheets, school applications, a matchmaker's questions over chai. Sometimes the boxes are there to help. Sometimes they decide who sits where, who marries whom, who drinks from which well. The tenth Guru lived in a world full of such boxes. In one stanza of Akal Ustat he lists them, one by one, and then picks up the very word the boxes were built on and gives it to everyone.
screen: `BOX ONE, BOX TWO, BOX THREE.` → `WHO SITS WHERE.` → `HE TAKES THE BOX WORD.`

segments.voice: Here is the stanza, in paraphrase. Someone has become a shaven-headed renouncer; someone a yogi; someone a celibate student; someone an ascetic. Some are Hindus, some Muslims; some are Shia, some Sunni. Then the line Sikhs quote today: recognize the whole human race as one. In Gurmukhi, manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo. Look at the word jat. In everyday speech it's the word for caste, the box you're born into, the one that decided so much. The Guru keeps the word and widens it until it holds everyone. There is one jat, and it is the human one. Notice the verb: pahichanbo, recognize. He doesn't say make everyone one, or pretend the labels aren't there. He has just named the renouncer, the yogi, the Hindu, the Muslim. The labels are real. The call is to recognize what's under them. Then the stanza turns toward God, in paraphrase: the Creator and the Merciful are the same; the Provider and the Compassionate are the same; there is no difference, and to think there is, is error. He uses names for God from more than one language, side by side, and says they point to one. In the Sikh tradition this line sits beside langar, where anyone eats sitting in the same row, and beside the gurdwara's open doors. It doesn't ask anyone to stop being who they are. It asks them to see one family when they look around the room.

1225.title: Same light in all
1225.hook: temple and mosque are the same, the forms of worship the same, all people one, though they look different (Akal Ustat 86)
1225.howItsDone: Sikhs sing and recite this stanza of Akal Ustat in kirtan and quote it when speaking of the oneness of humankind; it is read as teaching that one divine light lives in every person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one human race: manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo, recognize the whole human race as one. The labels are real, and the family under them is one.

In an anatomy class, the body on the table has no religion. The instructor points: here are the eyes, here the ears, here the lungs that took in air, here the heart. Nobody in the room can tell, from any of it, how this person prayed or which festival they loved. The next stanza of Akal Ustat goes to that same table. It names the places people pray, the clothes they wear, and then it looks underneath.
screen: `THE BODY ON THE TABLE.` → `EYES, EARS, LUNGS, HEART.` → `THE STANZA LOOKS UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: Akal Ustat, the very next stanza, in paraphrase. The temple and the mosque are the same; the Hindu worship and the Muslim prayer are the same. All people are one, though they appear many. Then a list of beings and peoples, and the reason they look different: it's the dress and custom of different lands. Then the anatomy lesson: the same eyes, the same ears, the same body, the same build. Each one a mix of earth and air, fire and water. And the stanza closes by setting names for God and books side by side and calling them the same. Yesterday's stanza was about the word for the human family. Today's is about what you see. Difference is real, the stanza says; it's the way a land dresses its people. But the eye and the ear and the four elements are shared. So the title for today, same light, is the stanza's conclusion carried one step: if the body is one stuff, the light that lives in it is one too. That's one way Sikhs read it, and it echoes a line in Sohila, in the Guru Granth Sahib: the One's light is in all. And it's a week's end, so look how the week has climbed. The world as a dream we wake from gently. The Name that remains when the dream ends. The Gurus' teachings closing, one teaching in many voices. Then a new block: the book of the Tenth, discussed with respect. Akal Ustat, praise that puts armies in scale. One human race. And now, under every robe and every rooftop, the same light.
screen: `TEMPLE AND MOSQUE, THE SAME.` · `DIFFERENT DRESS OF DIFFERENT LANDS.` · `SAME EYES, EARS, EARTH AND WATER.` · `A WEEK FROM DREAM TO LIGHT.` · then, large: `ALL THE SAME LIGHT.`

Then look underneath, the way the stanza does: their eyes, their ears, breath coming and going, the same air you're breathing now. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath.
